full_text:
On August 28, 1963, a quarter of a million citizens blanketed the National Mall in Washington D.C. for the historic March on Washington.

Standing on the marble steps of the Lincoln Memorial, thirty-four-year-old Baptist preacher Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. stepped to the podium.

Gospel singer Mahalia Jackson called out from behind him: "Tell them about the dream, Martin!"

King pushed his prepared text aside and spoke with prophetic grandeur:

**"I have a dream today!**

I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.'

I have a dream that on the red hills of Georgia, the sons of former slaves and the sons of former slave owners will be able to sit down together at the table of brotherhood!

**I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character!**

With this faith, we will be able to hew out of the mountain of despair a stone of hope!
With this faith, we will be able to transform the jangling discords of our nation into a beautiful symphony of brotherhood!"

The crowd roared with tears streaming down black and white faces alike.

King's dream galvanized the passage of the landmark Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965, forever establishing that human dignity transcends the artificial barrier of skin pigment.
moral: Character and virtue are the true measures of human worth; judging others by external appearance denies their divine humanity.
